notes.meaning: Bildad steps forward to give his second speech to Job. He has lost his patience and drops the gentle encouragement he offered earlier. Now he speaks with sharp irritation and prepares to deliver a severe warning.

Bildad asks Job when he will finally put an end to his long, empty speeches. He feels worn out by Job's self-defense and insists that Job must show some sense and listen. Only when Job stops arguing, Bildad claims, can a sensible conversation take place.

Bildad expresses deep offense at how Job has treated his friends. He asks why Job looks down on them as if they were dumb cattle without any understanding. Job had previously questioned their wisdom, and Bildad takes that insult to heart.

Bildad tells Job that his own uncontrolled anger is what is tearing him apart, not God. He asks whether Job really expects God to abandon the moral order of the world just to suit one man. In Bildad's view, God's justice is as fixed as a giant boulder and will not move for anyone.

Bildad uses the picture of a snuffed-out lamp and a dark tent to describe the fate of the wicked. In the ancient desert world, a fire and a hanging lamp were signs of hospitality, life, and domestic warmth. When God puts out a sinner's light, all his worldly prosperity and joy vanish into total gloom.

A wicked person may start out taking strong, confident strides, but his steps are soon cut short. His own clever schemes and sinful plans end up tripping him. Instead of succeeding, his plots become the very trap that brings him down.

Bildad piles up six different images of hunting gear, including nets, snares, nooses, and hidden pitfalls. He insists that the evil-doer brings about his own capture by walking right into danger with his own feet. Sin deceives the sinner, ensuring that God's judgment will seize him wherever he goes.

Sudden terrors surround the wicked person on every side, keeping him in constant panic. Guilt haunts his mind like an enemy chasing right behind his heels. He finds no peace anywhere, because an uneasy conscience makes him flee even when no one is chasing him.

The sinner's once-great strength is worn away by hunger and exhaustion. Complete ruin stands right next to him, ready to pounce the moment he stumbles. He has no stamina left to fight off the disasters closing in on him.

A horrific disease consumes the sinner's skin and devours his limbs. Bildad calls this sickness the firstborn of death, meaning the deadliest and most powerful ailment death can produce. This was a cruel, thinly veiled reference to the terrible skin disease Job was suffering from at that very moment.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that 'the firstborn of death' refers to Namtar, an ancient Mesopotamian god of pestilence and vizier of the underworld.

notes.meaning: The ungodly man is ripped away from the safe shelter of his home, where he felt secure. He is marched like a captive prisoner straight into the hands of the king of terrors. This king is death itself, the ultimate terror that strips away all earthly support.

Destruction takes over the wicked man's home because the tent is no longer his. Burning sulfur is scattered over his dwelling, recalling the judgment that wiped out the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah. Nothing good can remain where God's curse has fallen.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some interpreters read the first phrase of this verse as referring to Lilith, a night demon from ancient Mesopotamian lore, taking up residence in the abandoned tent.

notes.meaning: Bildad compares the wicked man to a tree that dries up completely. His roots wither underground and his top branches are cut off above. This was another harsh jab at Job, implying that the death of Job's children was proof that the family line was being cut off for sin.

All memory of the evil person disappears from the land after he dies. No one speaks his name with honor in the public streets or open country. His reputation rots away along with his body, leaving no trace behind.

The sinner is forcibly driven out of the bright light of life and pushed into the darkness of the grave. He desperately wants to stay, but the world is glad to be rid of him. Death banishes him completely from the land of the living.

No child, grandchild, or living relative remains to carry on the wicked man's name. His home is left entirely empty, without a single survivor. Bildad uses this point to deliver a painful blow to Job, whose sons and daughters had just perished.

People all across the world, from west to east, are shocked and horrified when they see the wicked man's downfall. Future generations shudder when they hear the story of such sudden, total ruin. His disaster becomes a frightening warning for everyone.

Bildad sums up his speech with a harsh, final verdict. He declares that this terrible end is exactly what happens to those who turn away from God and live in evil. By ending this way, Bildad leaves no doubt that he views Job as an ungodly man who does not know God at all.
